AccName 1.2 (step 2H, recursive name from content) recurses into the figure, so by the spec, and by ACT rule c487ae, the link's name is "Esquenta Black da Casa", which states its purpose. So in Chrome and Edge the name is empty and name-based tools such as voice control get nothing, while screen readers in browse mode usually still read the image's alt. Competent auditors split on whether a browser deviation on spec-valid markup fails 4.1.2, and I could not test assistive technology output here. captureDiffers: cannot_tell. message: The text "Encarregado pelo Tratamento de Dados Pessoais" has at most 3.11:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #00afef…#029bde), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Footer link text "Encarregado pelo Tratamento de Dados Pessoais", white on the light end of the footer gradient (#00afef behind much of it), best case 3.11:1, worst about 2.5:1, under 4.5:1. I re-measured the screenshot region: white glyphs on the darkest background pixel give about the same ratio, and it is 16px normal text, so 4.5:1 applies. The live theme CSS still sets the same colours, so the capture matches what users get. Live main.css: footer background linear-gradient(91deg, #0864b0, #00afef 80%), links white.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Footer text "Encarregado pelo Tratamento de Dados Pessoais", 16px weight 400, white on the footer's CSS background linear-gradient(91deg, #0864b0 0.23%, #00afef 80.21%), which the live style sheet still sets. Sampling the screenshot inside the element's box gives backgrounds of #029cdf to #00afef, about 2.51 to 3.08:1 against white, all below 4.5:1, and the text is neither large nor bold enough for 3:1, nor incidental or a logotype; no text-shadow or other technique raises it. The screenshot is fully styled and matches the live CSS, so the capture does not differ. The claim names the failure.

ref: #parte1ProcCNJ
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input class="field txtInput parte-1-proccnj form-control" id="parte1ProcCNJ" name="parte1ProcCNJ" placeholder="Num. única" title="Informe Primeira parte da numeração do processo" type="text" value="" accesskey="c" size="15" maxlength="25">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Case-number textbox #parte1ProcCNJ in the header search. Its label <label for> "Num. unica" has class d-none (display:none, confirmed in the live HTML); it also has a title and a placeholder. Chromium's own tree in the snapshot gives it name "" with a labelledby relation to that hidden label and no description: Blink takes the hidden label as the name source, gets empty text and does not fall back to the title or placeholder. So in Chrome/Edge, what most users run, the field has no accessible name, a 4.1.2 failure (HTML-AAM would fall back to the title, which is why code-only review or axe may pass it). The claim states exactly this; 'announces only textbox' is close (NVDA may still voice the placeholder). Live markup unchanged.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The first case-number textbox in the header ("Num. única"). Its <label for> is display:none (class d-none), and Chromium's tree (CDP) gives it the name "" with a labelledby relation to that hidden label, so the claim is true of the capture. But the input also has title="Informe Primeira parte da numeração do processo" and placeholder "Num. única": HTML-AAM lists the title, then the placeholder, as fallbacks when the label yields no text, H65 (title) is a sufficient technique for naming a control, and engines that follow that fallback (and axe's name computation) name it from the title. Whether users receive a name thus depends on the browser (none in Chromium, the title elsewhere), and competent auditors would disagree whether a title that the spec makes the name, but Chromium drops, meets 4.1.2. The live HTML has the same hidden label and attributes.

ref: #portlet_com_liferay_journal_content_web_portlet_JournalContentPortlet_INSTANCE_L0ti > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > div > div > h2:nth-of-type(1) > a:nth-of-type(3)
message: The link text "Link sem descrição" is shared by 4 links that lead to 4 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Link 3 of the tile row (to the Estatisticas/Relatorio SIC page). The four image links in the first h2 (Fale com a Ouvidoria -> ESOU form at www3, Perguntas mais frequentes -> FAQ page, Estatisticas -> statistics page, Balcao virtual -> Azure video-counter app) all carry aria-label="Link sem descricao", which overrides the descriptive alt of their images: Chromium's tree in the snapshot gives each link the name "Link sem descricao" (nameFrom aria-label) and the h2 itself reads "Link sem descricao" four times. No title or aria-describedby; they share the same h2 block, so their context is identical. I opened the four destinations on the live page: four different, non-equivalent pages. The icon tiles visibly tell them apart. By R1 the set fails, and the name itself ("link without description") does not describe any purpose either; 2.5.3 also fails (visible tile text not in the name). Live HTML still has the same four aria-labels (two hrefs are now absolute portaltj URLs, same pages), so the capture matches. The claim names this failure: true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the "Estatísticas" tile (href /web/guest/institucional/ouvidoria/estatisticas). The four image links in the first h2 of the content all carry aria-label="Link sem descrição", which overrides their images' alternatives: Chromium's tree (CDP) gives each link the name "Link sem descrição", nameFrom aria-label, and gives the h2 the name of four copies of it. None has a title or aria-describedby, and all four sit in the same h2 (their sentence, block and preceding heading at once), so nothing in the rubric's context list tells them apart: they form one R1 set. They lead to four non-equivalent resources (the ESOU manifestation form, the FAQ page, the statistics page and the Balcão Virtual meeting app), and the tiles visibly read "Fale com a Ouvidoria", "Perguntas mais Frequentes", "Estatísticas" and "Balcão Virtual" in the screenshot, so each link of the set fails 2.4.4 by R1; the shared name is also a placeholder that describes no purpose. I looked for a way out: the alternatives exist in the DOM and as image children in the tree, but the link's name is the aria-label, and that is what screen readers announce for the link. The live HTML still has the four aria-labels (the two internal hrefs are now absolute portaltj.tjrj.jus.br addresses, which changes nothing). The claim names this failure.

ref: #portlet_com_liferay_journal_content_web_portlet_JournalContentPortlet_INSTANCE_L0ti > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > div > div > h2:nth-of-type(1) > a:nth-of-type(1) > picture > img

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The 'Fale com a Ouvidoria' tile image, the only content of a link to the ESOU form. Its own alt ("Fale com a ouvidoria. Servico de informacao ao cidadao. Clique aqui") matches the tile text and would describe the purpose, but the link's aria-label "Link sem descricao" overrides it: Chromium names the link from aria-label, so the image link, a control, is announced with a name that does not describe its purpose. Read as the rubric frames 1.1.1 for image-only links (the control's name must describe its purpose) it fails; but the image's own text alternative is adequate and many auditors would log this only against the link (2.4.4, 4.1.2, 2.5.3), not 1.1.1. Competent auditors would split, so uncertain. Live HTML identical.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The "Fale com a Ouvidoria" tile image, the only content of a link to the ESOU form. Its own alt ("Fale com a ouvidoria. Serviço de informação ao cidadão. Clique aqui") matches the crop and would describe the link's purpose, and Chromium keeps the image in the tree with that name; but the link's aria-label "Link sem descrição" overrides it, so the image link, as a control, has the exposed name "Link sem descrição", which describes no purpose. Read as the rubric reads 1.1.1 for an image that is all a link holds (the control must have a name that describes its purpose), it fails; but the image's text alternative itself is accurate, and competent auditors would place this defect on the link (2.4.4, 4.1.2, and 2.5.3, since the visible label is not in the name) rather than on the image's alternative. Hence uncertain. The live HTML is the same.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header logo (it reads "PJERJ Poder Judiciário Estado do Rio de Janeiro"), the only content of a link to www.tjrj.jus.br/web/guest, the court's home page; Chromium names the link "Logo TJRJ" from the alt. ref: #__next > footer > section > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > form > div > input
subject: E-mail
message: The placeholder "E-mail" has a contrast of 4.40:1 with the field (#707097 on #f7f7f7). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" aria-label="E-mail" placeholder="E-mail" class="Newsletter_emailInput__XLU6p">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The newsletter E-mail field in the footer (transparent input over the #f7f7f7 footer, placeholder 'E-mail', 11-12px weight 300). The site's live stylesheet (chunk 0d5b24039af96206.css) sets .Newsletter_emailInput__XLU6p::placeholder{color:#707070}, and the screenshot's dominant background around the field is #f7f7f7; #707070 on #f7f7f7 is 4.62:1, which meets the 4.5:1 that 1.4.3 asks of small text. The snapshot's pixelContrast says foregroundFrom 'pixels', uniform false: the #707097 it reports is a blend picked from subpixel-antialiased glyph edges (the screenshot shows coloured fringes such as #7083b1 and #977070 there), not the text colour, so the claim's 4.40:1 is false. The capture matches what users get (same CSS, same footer); the error lies in the collector's colour sampling, so the cause is collector_error.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The newsletter E-mail field in the footer, whose placeholder "E-mail" is its visible label, so the placeholder is text under 1.4.3 (11px, weight 300, needs 4.5:1). The footer stylesheet the page loads (css chunk 0d5b24039af96206, footer chunk 2245) sets .Newsletter_emailInput__XLU6p::placeholder{color:#707070} on a transparent input over the #f7f7f7 footer. The screenshot agrees: zoomed, the placeholder glyphs are drawn with subpixel (coloured-fringe) antialiasing, every channel bottoms out at exactly 0x70 and the fully covered pixels are #707070, while #707097 is one of the fringe colours (#977070, #7083b1, #707097). #707070 on #f7f7f7 is 4.62:1, above 4.5:1. claimTrue: no, the stated colour and 4.40:1 are an antialiasing artefact of the pixel sample, not the text colour. elementFails: no. captureDiffers: no, the live CSS and the capture agree. Cause: the rule had a correct screenshot and took a fringe pixel for the text colour.

The product name h3 'Cinto De Couro Minibold' comes after it, inside a separate text link in a sibling div, so it is not in the image link's context (F63; R2), and only that visual card title would explain the link. So the link fails 2.4.4, and the claim that '1' does not match a destination titled 'Cinto De Couro Minibold' names that failure. The live page builds the same markup, so the capture matches.

skeptic.label: true_positive

ref: #input_1_4
message: The field "Company" asks for the user's company name, but autocomplete="new-password" says it holds their new password.

patch.ref: #input_1_4
patch.after: <input name="input_4" id="input_1_4" type="text" value="" autocomplete="organization">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The same Gravity Forms honeypot input, labelled 'Company', with autocomplete="new-password" and the visible-to-screen-readers instruction 'This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.' It does not ask for the user's company: it is a spam trap that must stay empty, and the new-password token only stops autofill. 1.3.5 covers input fields that collect information about the user. This one collects nothing, so the token mismatch is not a 1.3.5 failure. The model had the instruction in context and misread the field. The live markup is the same.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Field #input_1_4 is a Gravity Forms honeypot (class gfield--type-honeypot, description "This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged"), hidden off-screen. It does not ask for the user's company name. Its label is a decoy that changes on every load: "Company" in the capture, and Comments, Facebook, Instagram and Phone on my live loads. autocomplete="new-password" is Gravity Forms' way of stopping browsers from autofilling the trap. 1.3.5 covers fields that collect information about the user, and this one collects nothing, so it is out of scope and passes. The claim misreads the field's purpose. The label text differs from load to load, but that is the plugin's design, not a difference between the capture and what users receive.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Newsletter field 'Your Email Address*' (input type=email, Gravity Forms). It collects the user's own email, which is an Input Purpose (email). Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has an autocomplete attribute. type=email gives the data format but not that the address is the user's own. The sufficient technique H98 (autocomplete="email") is missing, so the field's purpose cannot be programmatically determined, and this fails 1.3.5 as claimed.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The newsletter field labelled "Your Email Address*" asks for the user's own email address, which is the input purpose "email". Its markup (`type="email"`, no autocomplete) does not identify that purpose: type="email" gives the data type, not the autofill purpose, and H98 needs the autocomplete token. I checked for an autocomplete added elsewhere and found none: the live HTML has the same input without it. The claim names the failure.

ref: #input_1_1
subject: Enter your email address
message: The placeholder "Enter your email address" has a contrast of 3.95:1 with the field (#808080 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input name="input_1" id="input_1_1" type="email" value="" class="large" placeholder="Enter your email address" aria-required="true" aria-invalid="false">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Placeholder 'Enter your email address' in the footer newsletter email field. The theme's main.min.css sets '.footer__subscribe-form input[type=email]::placeholder { color: #808080; font-size: 18px }', and the field background is white. That gives 3.95:1. The darkest pixels of the placeholder in the screenshot are #808080, which matches. The text is 18px at weight 400, so it is not large text and needs 4.5:1. Placeholder text is visible text that is neither incidental nor a logo. The live stylesheet is unchanged. This fails 1.4.3, as the claim says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The newsletter email field's placeholder "Enter your email address" is grey on the white field. The live theme CSS has `.footer__subscribe-form input[type=email]::placeholder { color: #808080; font-size: 18px }`, and #808080 on #ffffff works out to 3.95:1. At 18px and weight 400 it is not large text, so 4.5:1 applies. I looked for a way out and found none: a visible label "Your Email Address*" sits above, but 1.4.3 has no exception for placeholder text (it is not an inactive control, decoration, invisible, part of a picture or a logotype). The screenshot shows the styled page and the live CSS is the same, so the capture matches.

message: The text "info@dlrcoco.ie" has at most 4.43:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #566af6…#5569f6), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a background image). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Footer mailto link 'info@dlrcoco.ie', white, 14px bold (not large text). The footer is blue-500 with a decorative lighter logo swoosh (.logo-bkg). Screenshot pixels behind the address are #566af5 (4.40:1) to #5569f3 (4.47:1); only the 'E-mail:' label lies on the darker #435af5. That is below 4.5:1 at the 1280px viewport. The screenshot's vertical offset differs from the snapshot bounds, but the footer colours are the same and the live markup is unchanged. The claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The footer link 'info@dlrcoco.ie' is white, 14px bold, so it is not large text and needs 4.5:1. The footer is tw-bg-blue-500 with a decorative 'logo-bkg' overlay. I sampled the screenshot pixels: behind the address they are #566af5 to #5568f2, which gives 4.40-4.52:1 against white. Only the far right end reaches the darker #4259f4 (5.3:1). So most of the text is under 4.5:1, and Understanding 1.4.3 forbids rounding. My only reasons for doubt are that the margin is thin and the overlay's position depends on viewport width. Neither changes what users see at the captured width, and the live footer markup is the same.

ref: #edit-keys
subject: Search for anything...
message: The placeholder "Search for anything..." has a contrast of 2.54:1 with the field (#9ca3af on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input data-drupal-selector="edit-keys" data-search-api-autocomplete-search="search" class="form-autocomplete form-text ui-autocomplete-input" data-autocomplete-path="/search_api_autocomplete/search?display=page_1&&filter=keys" type="text" id="edit-keys" name="keys" value="" size="30" maxlength="128" placeholder="Search for anything..." data-once="autocomplete search-api-autocomplete" autocomplete="off">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Search field #edit-keys with the placeholder 'Search for anything...'. The darkest glyph pixel in the screenshot is #9ca3af (the Tailwind placeholder colour) on white, which is 2.54:1, well below 4.5:1 for 16px regular text. Placeholder text is text, not an inactive component, and here it is the field's only visible prompt. The live page has the same field and styles. The claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The hero search field #edit-keys has the placeholder 'Search for anything...'. The field has no label, and the placeholder is its only instruction. Sampling the screenshot pixels confirms the placeholder renders as #9ca3af on #ffffff, which is 2.54:1. I checked whether placeholder text could be exempt. Understanding 1.4.3 says the criterion 'applies to text in the page, including placeholder text', and none of the incidental exceptions apply, so it needs 4.5:1. The live input is the same.

patch.to: Find out more about Transforming Dundrum project
patch.after: Find out more about Transforming Dundrum project

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: [visual context] 'Find out more' button link (CSS uppercase) to the Transforming Dundrum project page. The visual label 'Transforming Dundrum:' is a <div> inside a styled <span>, not a heading, and the descriptive paragraphs are separate blocks. The link sits alone in its own div, with no title or aria-describedby. The nearest preceding heading is the unrelated news card h2 '€335 Million Budget Adopted...', which also precedes that card's own 'Find out more' link to a different page. So the purpose cannot be determined from the link and its programmatic context. Live HTML is the same. The claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: [visual context] The 'Find out more' button (shown as 'FIND OUT MORE') leads to the Transforming Dundrum page. The 'Transforming Dundrum:' title above it is a styled span > div, not a heading, and the description paragraphs are separate elements. The link sits alone in its own div, with no title or aria-describedby. The heading just before it is the unrelated news h2 '€335 Million Budget Adopted…', which is also the preceding heading of that news card's own 'Find out more' link. So nothing in the rubric's programmatic context gives the purpose, and only the visual title explains it. That fails 2.4.4 under the fixed reading. The live HTML is the same. The claim's 'nothing around it' holds for the context that counts.

ref: #block-dlrd9-main-menu > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
subject: Gaeilge
message: "Gaeilge" is in Irish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="ga" to the link.

patch.ref: #block-dlrd9-main-menu > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
patch.after: <a href="#gaeilge" lang="ga">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Top-menu link 'Gaeilge' (href #gaeilge, the Recite Me Irish-translation trigger) has no lang attribute and inherits lang=en. Understanding 3.1.2's 'Alternative language links' example gives exactly this pattern, a language's name written in that language, marked with lang. An English voice mispronounces 'Gaeilge', so the vernacular exception does not apply in practice. Live HTML has the same markup in both menus. The claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: 'Gaeilge' in the top menu is the Recite Me Irish-translation switcher (li#reciteIrishTranslation, href #gaeilge). Neither the link nor any ancestor has lang="ga", so it inherits the page's lang="en". The live HTML matches. I considered whether it could pass as a proper name, a vernacular word or a single word. Understanding 3.1.2 lists 'Alternative language links' as an example whose language must be marked with lang, and its pronunciation test fails: English speech output does not say 'Gaeilge' as Irish does. So the element fails 3.1.2, as the claim says.

subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale:
Card link to /node/61762 ('Councillors & Democracy'). It wraps an
with an SVG icon and the visible text. In Chrome's accessibility tree in the snapshot, the link's name is empty. The live HTML has the same
...

AccName would include the text and Firefox may expose it, but the pattern is not accessibility supported in the dominant engine, so the name cannot be programmatically determined there. The claim names that failure.

The spec computation would yield the text, but the browser most users run exposes no name, so 4.1.2 fails there. The live HTML is identical, and the claim names that failure.

Its alt is 'test logo'. claimTrue: yes, that is a placeholder label and not what the image conveys. elementFails: users of the alternative lose the Irish name and the Trinity College partnership the image states; placeholder text is F30. subject: Adult Services 14.09.2023

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the stock photo (blood sample tubes on a hospital form) in the sub-navigation tile link 'Adult Services'; its alt 'Adult Services 14.09.2023' is the CMS media item's title with its upload date. claimTrue: the alt is a label, not a description of what the image shows. elementFails: read in place of the image the link becomes 'Adult Services 14.09.2023 Adult Services'; the date is not an alternative for anything in the image (F30), and the photo, which adds nothing to the link text, should be alt="" (F38). It fails 1.1.1, and 'names a label, not what the image conveys here' names that defect in good faith. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same img and alt.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The img (alt "Adult Services 14.09.2023") is the photo of blood-sample tubes on a hospital form on the 'Adult Services' tile, inside a link whose visible text is 'Adult Services'. The claim is true of the capture: the alt is an upload label with a date, not a description. The live HTML is identical. Against the claim: the photo is redundant to the link text, so the WCAG fix is a null alt (F39), not a description of what the image conveys, and the alt's words 'Adult Services' do echo the tile's subject. The date makes it noise in the link name, so a failure is likely, but whether the claim's 'not what the image conveys' names the null-alt failure, and whether a topical alt in a labelled link fails at all, are points competent auditors would split on, so uncertain.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The placeholder "ex.: João da Silva Gomes" in the Nome field is visible text on a white field. The live CSS sets ::placeholder to the inherited text color (body hsl(220,4%,14%), about #222325) at opacity .6 and italic, which comes out near #7a7b7c on white, about 4.3:1. My pixel check of the screenshot found the darkest placeholder pixels around #838384, about 3.7-3.8:1. Both are below the 4.5:1 that 1.4.3 requires for 14px regular text, and placeholder text has no exception, so elementFails is yes. claimTrue is no: the ratio is about right, but the stated foreground #f1f1f1 is wrong (the text is mid-grey, and #f1f1f1 on white would be about 1.1:1). skeptic.label: uncertain

ref: html > body > header > div > div:nth-of-type(5) > a:nth-of-type(2)
subject: English
message: "English" is in English, but it inherits the page's language (pt-BR): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="en" to the link.

patch.after: <a href="/salasp/en" data-astro-cid-3ef6ksr2="" lang="en">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header language switcher link "English" (href /salasp/en) has no lang attribute, and neither do its ancestors, so it inherits html lang="pt-BR". "English" is an English word, not a proper name or a Portuguese vernacular word (Portuguese says "Inglês"), and Understanding 3.1.2's alternative-language-links example (H58) says to mark each language name with its language. The element fails 3.1.2, and the claim says why (claimTrue yes). The live HTML is the same: English with no lang (captureDiffers no).

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The visible header language switcher reads 'Português | English | Español'; the link 'English' (href /salasp/en) has no lang attribute and inherits html lang='pt-BR' (same in the live HTML; the duplicate links in the closed menu also lack lang). Understanding 3.1.2 says a single word can be subject to the criterion and that single words count as the surrounding language 'unless it is clear that a change in language was intended'. In a language switcher, where each name is written in its own language on purpose, the change is clearly intended. A language name used to address readers of that language is not a proper name, a technical term or a Portuguese vernacular word, and a pt-BR voice reads 'English' with Portuguese rules. None of the skeptic's candidate reasons holds, so this is a 3.1.2 failure and the claim names it.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the body text of the DPOeasy cookie banner, rendered in an open shadow root: 'We use cookies to personalize your experience...'. The page is html lang=pt-br, and neither the banner host nor any banner node has a lang attribute, so the English passage is read as Portuguese. That is a 3.1.2 failure, and the claim names it. I checked the live banner.js. It picks its strings from navigator.language and ships pt, en and es sets. It never sets lang. The capture matches what a visitor with an English-language browser gets today. Visitors whose browser is in Portuguese get Portuguese strings, so they do not meet this failure, but English-locale browsers are ordinary browsers, and for them the unmarked English passage is real.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the description paragraph of the DPOnet cookie banner (shadow DOM in #dpoeasy-banner). In the capture its text is English and nothing in the shadow tree carries lang, so it inherits html lang='pt-br'. The claim is true of the capture. However, the live banner.js picks its strings from navigator.language when no locale is configured: an exact or base-language match among pt-br, en-us and es-es, falling back to pt-br. It ships 'Usamos cookies para personalizar sua experiência...' for pt-BR. Rampa's browser had an English locale, so it got the English strings. A visitor with a Portuguese browser, the site's audience, receives Portuguese text that matches the page language and passes. A visitor with an en-* browser gets unmarked English and would fail. Which variant counts as 'the page users receive' is a call auditors would reasonably split on, so the label is uncertain.

message: The icon of this button has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the fixed floating support button (img alt 'Abrir Central de Suporte'). Its only content is an SVG that I downloaded from the live site: the WhatsApp logo, a white phone-in-speech-bubble (fill #fff) on the site's background-color:#25d366 circle. The screenshot shows that brand mark at the bottom right. The sentence is true of the capture: white on #25d366 is 1.98:1, and the icon is all the button shows. But this is WhatsApp's logo in its own brand colours, white glyph on WhatsApp green. Understanding 1.4.11 says under the essential exception that 'The brand logo of an organization or product ... is generally presented in the brand's specific colors; it is therefore exempt', and that for a logo that is the only visible content of a control 'normatively the exemption "carries over" to the user interface component'. Using a higher-contrast variant is encouraged there, not required. So the button does not fail 1.4.11. The rule measured the right pixels but applied G207's 3:1 to an exempt logo. I compared the live HTML (same button, CSS and SVG) and found no difference that matters.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the fixed 60px support button ('Abrir Central de Suporte'). Its only content is an SVG of the WhatsApp glyph, painted white (#fff), on the button's CSS background-color #25d366. The screenshot shows a white WhatsApp glyph on a green disc. White on #25d366 is 1.98:1 and the glyph is all the control shows, so the claim holds of the capture. The live page serves the same button, CSS and SVG, so captureDiffers is no. The skeptic's reason is the logo exemption. Understanding 1.4.11 says 'Logos and logotypes: The brand logo of an organization or product ... is generally presented in the brand's specific colors; it is therefore exempt'. It also says that 'normatively the exemption "carries over" to the user interface component', and that choosing a higher-contrast variant is only encouraged. The glyph is the WhatsApp logo in WhatsApp's own brand green and white, its normal presentation rather than a dimmed author choice. Read that way, the element does not fail, which is my elementFails. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree, though. The button opens a support centre, so the third-party logo works as a generic chat icon and does not represent the site's organisation. Some auditors also hold that icons on controls must reach 3:1 whatever the brand. The rubric fixes neither reading, so the label is uncertain.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The visible top-menu link 'Cymraeg' (Welsh for 'Welsh') leads to the Welsh version of the page; the snapshot shows no lang attribute on it or any ancestor except html lang="en", so the claim holds of the capture. The raw HTML of the live page has the same markup (title="Cymraeg", no lang, html lang="en"), so the capture matches what users get. Understanding 3.1.2 covers this case in its 'Alternative language links' example, where each link's text is the language's name in that language and carries lang (e.g. lang="fr" on 'Français'). A language name in a switcher is not treated as an exempt proper name there. The link fails 3.1.2 for the reason the claim gives.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The top-menu link 'Cymraeg' (the Welsh name of Welsh, title='Cymraeg') points to the Welsh version of the page (/cy-gb/gwirior-gofrestr/). In the snapshot, neither the link nor any ancestor carries a lang attribute, so it inherits html lang='en', and the claim holds. I tested the skeptic's counter-arguments. The proper-name exception does not hold up: the endonym is not used unchanged across languages (English says 'Welsh'), and it is shown here precisely because it is Welsh. The single-word guidance in Understanding 3.1.2 applies only 'unless it is clear that a change in language was intended', and a language switcher to the Welsh version makes that intent clear. Understanding 3.1.2's own 'Alternative language links' example marks each language name with lang (lang='de' Deutsch, and so on), which is exactly this pattern. On the live page (curl, 2026-11-21) the markup is the same and still has no lang; the hidden mobile-menu copy also lacks one. So the capture does not differ, the element fails 3.1.2, and the claim names that failure.

ref: #main-content > div:nth-of-type(2) > section:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > article:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
subject: Man fighting for his life after early-morning assault outside Bristol bar
message: The text alternative "Man fighting for his life after early-morning assault outside Bristol bar" describes something the image does not show.
evidence: Man fighting for his life after early-morning assault outside Bristol bar

patch.ref: #main-content > div:nth-of-type(2) > section:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > article:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
patch.from: Man fighting for his life after early-morning assault outside Bristol bar
patch.to: Street view of a row of shops and buildings in Bristol.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: A teaser photo in the top section: a street-level screenshot of a terraced shopping street with a bar front and parked vans, presumably the scene of the assault. claimTrue: yes. The alt 'Man fighting for his life after early-morning assault outside Bristol bar' describes nothing the picture shows. The image is not inside a link: it sits in the teaser's cover div, and the headline is a separate link (an h3) right beside it in the same article. Its alt copies that headline word for word. What the picture does convey, the street where it happened, is not in the alt. My own reading is that it fails 1.1.1. A photo shown next to its own headline is either decoration, in which case it should be hidden from assistive technology (alt=""), or it carries information, in which case the alt should describe the picture. A copy of the headline does neither: screen reader users hear the headline twice and get nothing of what the picture shows. Competent auditors do reasonably disagree here, though. Many accept a teaser thumbnail whose alt names the story it illustrates, or treat the repeat as a best-practice issue rather than a 1.1.1 failure, so the label is uncertain. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same img, alt and src, and the screenshot shows the same photo.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the teaser photo for 'Man fighting for his life after early-morning assault outside Bristol bar'. The crop shows a street of shopfronts with a parked van, apparently the location, with no person or incident visible. The alt is the headline and describes what the photo does not show, so the claim is true of the capture. The image is not inside a link: it sits in the teaser's cover wrapper, and the headline is a separate h3 link right after it with the same text. Competent auditors split on teaser photos whose alt repeats the headline: one reading takes the photo as illustrative, so the alt should describe it, and the headline does not; a second takes it as redundant or decorative, which calls for alt="" (F38 fails any non-null alt on a purely decorative img); a third holds that the alt still serves the photo's purpose in a teaser (saying which story it illustrates) and that the repetition is a redundancy issue (axe treats it as best practice), not a 1.1.1 failure. The evidence does not settle which reading applies, so elementFails is cannot_tell and the label is uncertain. The live page (fetched 2026-11-21) serves the same img, alt and teaser markup, and the screenshot is a styled render, so captureDiffers is no.

message: The field "Nome Completo" asks for the user's full name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="name" is missing.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the required "Nome Completo" input in the "Tem mais alguma dúvida?" lead form, which asks for the visitor's own contact details. In both the snapshot (post-script DOM) and the live HTML, it has a label, a title and a type, but no autocomplete attribute. The field collects information about the user with a purpose listed in WCAG's Input Purposes (name), and HTML supports autocomplete, so 1.3.5 requires the purpose to be programmatically determinable, which H98 provides. skeptic.label: true_positive

Neither the snapshot nor the live page (server HTML and the DOM after scripts in headless Edge 158, 2026-11-21) has an autocomplete attribute on the input or the form, so claimTrue is yes. Looking for a pass: the field's type only sets the data format, not that the value is the user's own, and 1.3.5's sufficient technique H98 needs the autocomplete token ('name'); the id, title and label do not identify the purpose programmatically. elementFails is yes, captureDiffers is no. True positive.

ref: #header > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > div
subject: aria-labelledby=dropdown09
message: 8 elements have id="dropdown09": this element's name comes from the first of them ("Cursos"), not from the one beside it ("Modalidades"). Give each a unique id.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the Modalidades dropdown panel, a div with no role (generic) and aria-labelledby="dropdown09". The snapshot and the live HTML both have eight header buttons with id="dropdown09", and Chrome resolves the reference to the first one (the Cursos button), so the sentence is true of the capture. It is not a 4.1.2 failure of this element, though. The panel is a container, not a user interface component, and ARIA 1.2 prohibits names on the generic role, so screen readers do not normally announce its name. Also, every one of the eight buttons has aria-label="Fechar menu", so the panel's name is "Fechar menu" (the captured browser name) whichever button the reference reaches. Unique ids would give exactly the same name, and the duplicate changes nothing users receive. Understanding 4.1.1 (WCAG 2.1) treats parsing as always satisfied for HTML, and says incorrect names caused by a duplicate id fall under other criteria. No incorrect name comes from the duplicate here. The real defect is elsewhere: the buttons' aria-label "Fechar menu" replaces their visible text, which fails 2.5.3 and makes their names misleading. The live HTML matches the capture.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the generic dropdown panel (div.dropdown-menu, no role) under the 'Modalidades' top-nav button, with aria-labelledby="dropdown09". The capture and the live page (server HTML and a headless Edge 158 render on 2026-11-21) both have eight buttons with id="dropdown09", and the browser resolves the reference to the first one (the 'Cursos' button), so the sentence holds, read with the parentheses as the buttons' visible text; the name string itself is 'Fechar menu', not 'Cursos'. elementFails is no: the panel is a generic container, not a user interface component that needs a name (ARIA 1.2 prohibits naming the generic role, and screen readers do not announce it). The duplicate id also changes nothing users get: every one of the eight buttons has aria-label="Fechar menu", so with unique ids each panel would get the same name 'Fechar menu'. Duplicate ids are a WCAG 2.1 4.1.1 (F77) issue, and the buttons' shared aria-label 'Fechar menu' (a 'close menu' name on collapsed triggers) is a 4.1.2/2.5.3 problem on the buttons, but neither is this panel failing 4.1.2. captureDiffers is no: the live page matches. False positive: the rule treats a duplicate-id reference on a nameless-by-design container as a 4.1.2 naming failure.

The live HTML is identical. The captured Chrome accessibility tree gives the link an empty name with no name source, while it named the other links normally. So the claim is true of the capture, apparently because Chromium does not take a figure's content into a link's name. By the accessible name computation, the name comes from the author-supplied content (the alt and the figcaption, through recursive name from content) and, failing that, from the title. An auditor reading the markup, or using an accname-based tool such as axe, would find a name and pass 4.1.2. An auditor testing Chrome's tree or a screen reader on Chrome may hear only "link" and fail it as not accessibility-supported. I could not run a browser to confirm what Chrome or Edge users get today, so elementFails is cannot_tell and the label is uncertain.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 70x70 promotional badge (selo-BF-op-02_29-10-25.png) overlaid on the product card for "Vestido longo est lumiere". Its crop and the full screenshot show an image of the words "BEST FRIDAY"; its alt is "selo-produto" ("product seal"), a generic placeholder naming the kind of element. claimTrue: yes, the alt names a label/type and not the content. elementFails: yes; the badge is informative (it tells the user the product is part of the Best Friday campaign, which no text in the card says: the card's text is only the name, sizes, "60 %", prices and "VER PRODUTO"), and an alt that does not convey that content fails 1.1.1 (F30, alt that is not an alternative). It is not the only content of the link (the link also holds the product photo and name), so R2 does not apply; even if one called it decorative, a non-null alt would still fail (F39). captureDiffers: no; the live HTML fetched today still carries the product flag markup for the listing's products, and the screenshot is fully styled. The claim names the real failure: true positive.

The claim names the real defect, so true_positive.

ref: #nomeNews
message: The field "Digite seu nome" asks for the user's full name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="name" is missing.

patch.ref: #nomeNews
patch.before: <input type="text" id="nomeNews" class="cantao-app-newsletter-home-0-x-input_new" required="" placeholder="Digite seu nome" name="nome">
patch.after: <input type="text" id="nomeNews" class="cantao-app-newsletter-home-0-x-input_new" required="" placeholder="Digite seu nome" name="nome" autocomplete="name">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the footer newsletter field <input type="text" id="nomeNews" name="nome" placeholder="Digite seu nome">, under the visible text "Nome". claimTrue: yes; it asks for the user's own name and has no autocomplete attribute. elementFails: yes; the user's name is a listed input purpose (name), the field collects information about the user, and its purpose is not programmatically determinable (no autocomplete token, H98 not met), so it fails 1.3.5. captureDiffers: no; the live server HTML fetched today has the same input without autocomplete. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the name field of the footer newsletter sign-up form (input id nomeNews, type text, name='nome', placeholder 'Digite seu nome', visual label 'Nome'). claimTrue: it asks for the subscriber's own name and has no autocomplete attribute. elementFails: name is a listed input purpose and HTML supports autocomplete; without autocomplete='name' (or given-name) nothing makes the purpose programmatically determinable, so it fails 1.3.5. Whether the shop wants the full or only the given name changes which token fits, not the failure. Looked for an exception: the field is about the user, and no other technique is used. captureDiffers: the live server HTML has the same input, with no autocomplete. true_positive.

ref: #emailNews
message: The field "Digite seu e-mail" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.after: <input type="mail" id="emailNews" class="cantao-app-newsletter-home-0-x-input_new" required="" placeholder="Digite seu e-mail" name="email" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the footer newsletter field <input type="mail" id="emailNews" name="email" placeholder="Digite seu e-mail">, under the visible text "E-mail" in a form inviting the user to sign up with their own name and e-mail. claimTrue: yes; it has no autocomplete attribute (type="mail" is not even a valid type, so it falls back to text), and the snapshot records Chromium's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError for it, so the Chromium remark also holds. elementFails: yes; it collects the user's e-mail, a purpose listed in WCAG's Input Purposes (email), and nothing makes that purpose programmatically determinable (no autocomplete, H98 not met). captureDiffers: no; the live server HTML fetched today has the same input, still without autocomplete. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the e-mail field of the footer newsletter sign-up form (input id emailNews, type='mail', name='email', placeholder 'Digite seu e-mail', visual label 'E-mail' in a p element). claimTrue: it collects the user's own e-mail address and has no autocomplete attribute; the snapshot records Chromium's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError for it, so the Chromium part holds too. elementFails: e-mail is one of the listed input purposes and HTML supports autocomplete, so 1.3.5 needs the purpose to be programmatically determinable; type='mail' is not a valid type (it falls back to text) and name='email' is not a means user agents rely on, so nothing identifies the purpose (H98 not met). Looked for an exception: the field asks about the user, not a third party, and no other technique is used. captureDiffers: the live server HTML has the same input, with no autocomplete. true_positive.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the "Switch to grid-2 layout" option (role=radio, aria-checked=false, enabled) of the product-grid layout switcher at the top right of the listing; its only content is an SVG of squares filled with currentColor. claimTrue: yes; sampling the screenshot at its bounds gives the icon #f3eaea on the background #fafafa, 1.13:1, and the icon is all the control shows. elementFails: yes; the icon is the visual information needed to identify this control and it is far below 3:1 against the adjacent colour (it is barely visible in the screenshot, while the selected grid-4 icon is near black at about 17:1). An unselected option is not an inactive (disabled) component, so the exception does not apply. captureDiffers: no; the screenshot is fully styled and the live server HTML has the same three buttons with grid-4 selected and this one unselected. True positive.

skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Switch to grid-2 layout' radio button in the gallery layout switcher, an unselected option (aria-checked=false) whose only visible content is an SVG grid icon. claimTrue: the screenshot crop shows the grid-2 and grid-3 icons as pale pink on the near-white page while the selected grid-4 icon is black; the live style sheet GridLayoutIcon.min.css sets the icon colour to #f3eaea, and to #181615 only for the --selected option, and #f3eaea on #fafafa computes to 1.13:1. elementFails: the icon is the visual information needed to identify the control, it is under 3:1, and the button is operable (not disabled, so the inactive exception does not apply); no hover or other rule raises it. ref: #slick-slide00 > img
subject: Boomtown 2 nov24
message: The text alternative "Boomtown 2 nov24" names a label, not what the image conveys here.

patch.ref: #slick-slide00 > img
patch.to: Two men examining a long, illuminated display of a historical map or document.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the first real slide of the experiences carousel (#slick-slide00, slick-current, aria-hidden false at capture), a photo of two older visitors looking at an illuminated exhibit case, with the caption 'The Titanic Experience'. It is not in a link. Its alt 'Boomtown 2 nov24' is an asset/campaign label, not a description of what the photo shows or why it is there, so the claim is true of the capture. A label like this is a text alternative that is not an alternative (F30); even a decorative reading would need a null alt. The element fails 1.1.1 for the reason the claim gives. The live HTML carries the same alt; the screenshot shows another slide only because the carousel rotates, which does not touch the claim.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the first slide (slick-slide00, the current slide at capture) of the Experiences carousel: two visitors at an illuminated display case in the Titanic Experience, with the caption 'The Titanic Experience'. Its alt 'Boomtown 2 nov24' is a media-library label: a gallery name, an index and a date. I checked whether 'Boomtown' could carry the meaning, since Boomtown Belfast is a real gallery of the Experience and the posters in the photo fit it. But '2 nov24' is file noise, and the string as a whole does not convey what the photo shows. If the image is informative, this is F30. If it only supplements the caption, it should have a null alt, and this announced label cannot be ignored (Situation F). Either way it fails 1.1.1. The live HTML has the same alt. The screenshot shows a later slide only because the carousel auto-advances, which does not affect this claim. The claim names the failure.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the only content of the link to /visitor-information/offers-events/white-star-premium-pass (the red arrow is a CSS span with no text). It shows the Titanica statue against the sky, and its alt 'Titanica BQ' names the statue plus a code; it does not identify the destination, the White Star Premium Pass offer page (whose title, h1 and description never mention Titanica). The h3 'White Star Premium Pass' above the card is a heading, not part of the link and not the image's alternative; per the rubric (R2, H30) a nearby heading or title does not cure 1.1.1 for an image that is all a link holds. The link has no title. The claim is true of the capture and names the failure. The live HTML is identical.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the only content of the link to /visitor-information/offers-events/white-star-premium-pass. Its alt 'Titanica BQ' names the Titanica sculpture in the photo, plus a code. In the live HTML the link also holds an empty span.c-arrow, which adds no text, and the link has no aria-label or title, so the link's name is 'Titanica BQ'. The destination page is 'White Star Premium Pass', and the alt does not identify it. Under H30 and the rubric's R2, the h3 'White Star Premium Pass' before the card may help 2.4.4, but it does not cure 1.1.1 for an image that is a link's only content. I found no technique that makes this pass. The live page matches the capture. The claim names the failure.

Its alt 'Untitled Design' is a leftover file/design name: it says nothing the map shows, so the claim, read in good faith, is true of the capture. The map conveys where the venue sits relative to landmarks and transport; the adjacent paragraph and the Google Maps link give only part of that. Placeholder text as an alternative is failure F30, and even if the map were judged decorative the non-empty placeholder alt would still be announced, so the element fails 1.1.1. Its alt 'Untitled Design' is a default file name (the image file is untitled-design.jpg), and it names nothing the map shows, so the claim holds of the capture. I looked for reasons it could pass. The text beside it gives only a general location ('heart of Titanic Quarter, short walk from the city centre'), not the map's landmarks and roads. The Google Maps link is another control, not a text alternative. Even if the map were taken as decorative, a non-null placeholder alt is still announced, so it cannot be ignored. This is F30 (placeholder or file name used as the alternative). The live HTML has the same img and alt. Read in good faith, the claim names the placeholder failure.

Capture does not differ. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether this is a 4.1.2 failure of the content: by the accessible name algorithm the figure is traversed and the name is the image's alt, axe-style checkers compute that name, and screen readers in browse mode read the image inside the link; others go by the name the browser exposes, which is empty in Chromium. skeptic.label: uncertain

I reproduced this in Edge 158 headless (Chromium): an img with alt inside a figure inside a link gives the link an empty name, while the same img without the figure, or inside a div, gives the alt. So the empty name is Chromium's real computation, not a collector artefact. Against it: under the accname algorithm (recursion into descendants, steps 2F/2H) and in spec-based checkers such as axe, the figure's img alt contributes, so the link would be named by the alt; screen readers in browse mode also read the inner graphic, so 'announces only link' overstates it. Whether spec-conformant markup that the dominant engine fails to name counts as a 4.1.2 failure is a point competent auditors would dispute, so I cannot say the element fails, and the label is uncertain. Even if the alt were taken as the name, it describes the photo rather than the destination, which is a 1.1.1/2.4.4 matter (R2), not this claim. The live HTML has the same markup (tabindex=-1, figure-wrapped img, no aria-label or title); images were lazy-loaded (state broken in the snapshot, loaded in the screenshot), which does not change the name, so captureDiffers is no.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The news card category label "Dica de Saúde" is a <span> styled by .blog .posts .box .texto span in the theme's style.css (live, 2026-11-21): color #FFF on background #0078D7, font-size .9em (14.4 px), weight 500, so normal-size text needing 4.5:1. I computed the ratio from the CSS values: relative luminance of #0078D7 is 0.1834, giving 1.05/0.2334 = 4.499:1. Understanding 1.4.3 says computed values are not rounded and that 4.499:1 does not meet 4.5:1. The label sits above the card's gradient overlay (the .texto flex item has z-index 1), and the screenshot shows white text on the solid blue chip, so the pixel measurement matches the CSS: claimTrue yes, elementFails yes. The live HTML and CSS are the same as the capture, so captureDiffers is no. True positive, if only just.

skeptic.label: true_positive

The text is not large (under 18pt, and not 14pt bold), so 4.5:1 applies, and Understanding 1.4.3 says the computed value is not rounded ("4.499:1 would not meet the 4.5:1 threshold"). I checked whether the page's 'Contraste' toggle could make it pass by G174: its script adds .bgdark to body and #home .blog and .textdark to p, a, h1-h5 and li, but leaves this span's own #0078D7 background and #FFF text unchanged, so the alternate presentation keeps 4.499:1. The label is real text, not a logo or an inactive control. The claim states the right colours and a ratio just under 4.5:1 ('at most 4.49' is the truncated 4.499), and the element fails 1.4.3.

message: The text "Comunicado" has at most 4.49:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #0078d7), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The news card category label "Comunicado" is a <span> styled by .blog .posts .box .texto span in the theme's style.css (live, 2026-11-21): color #FFF on background #0078D7, font-size .9em (14.4 px), weight 500, so normal-size text needing 4.5:1. I computed the ratio from the CSS values: relative luminance of #0078D7 is 0.1834, giving 1.05/0.2334 = 4.499:1. Understanding 1.4.3 says computed values are not rounded and that 4.499:1 does not meet 4.5:1. The label sits above the card's gradient overlay (the .texto flex item has z-index 1), and the screenshot shows white text on the solid blue chip, so the pixel measurement matches the CSS: claimTrue yes, elementFails yes. The live HTML and CSS are the same as the capture, so captureDiffers is no. True positive, if only just.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'Comunicado' category label on the third news card. The live HTML fetched on 2026-11-21 and the styled screenshot match the snapshot for this element. The theme's style.css (.blog .posts .box .texto span) sets color #FFF on background #0078D7, font-size .9em (14.4px at the 16px default), weight 500, uppercase, so the pixel measurement matches the CSS: the ratio is 4.499:1. The text is not large (under 18pt, and not 14pt bold), so 4.5:1 applies, and Understanding 1.4.3 says the computed value is not rounded ("4.499:1 would not meet the 4.5:1 threshold"). I checked whether the page's 'Contraste' toggle could make it pass by G174: its script adds .bgdark to body and #home .blog and .textdark to p, a, h1-h5 and li, but leaves this span's own #0078D7 background and #FFF text unchanged, so the alternate presentation keeps 4.499:1. The label is real text, not a logo or an inactive control. The claim states the right colours and a ratio just under 4.5:1 ('at most 4.49' is the truncated 4.499), and the element fails 1.4.3.

ref: #home > section:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a
subject: SAIBA MAIS
message: The link text "SAIBA MAIS" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

patch.ref: #home > section:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a
patch.to: Saiba mais sobre a Santa Casa JF
patch.after: Saiba mais sobre a Santa Casa JF

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The second "Saiba mais" link (<a href="" class="cta mt-5">), at the bottom of the "Conheça a Santa Casa JF" column. The claim says nothing around it explains it, but the nearest heading before it in document order is the h2 "Conheça a Santa Casa JF" in the same column, which this round counts as context (H80). With it, the link reads as 'learn more about Santa Casa JF', so claimTrue is no. The defect the element really has is a different one: its href is empty, so it just reloads the home page for every user (the live HTML of 2026-11-21 is the same). That is a broken link affecting all users alike, not missing link context, so I answer elementFails no for 2.4.4. Even an auditor who scored the empty href as a 2.4.4 failure would be scoring a reason this claim does not name. It shares its name with the PLASC "Saiba mais" link, but the different preceding headings tell them apart, so they are not one R1 set. The screenshot and live page match the capture: captureDiffers no. False positive: the model overlooked the preceding heading.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Saiba mais' button (<a href="" target="" class="cta mt-5">) under 'Conheça a Santa Casa JF'. The live HTML fetched on 2026-11-21 and the styled screenshot match the snapshot for this element, including the empty href; no script on the page handles it, so activating it only reloads the home page. The claim says nothing around the link tells where it goes, but the h2 'Conheça a Santa Casa JF' is the nearest heading before it, which this round counts as context, so 'Saiba mais' reads as 'learn more about the Santa Casa JF': the ground the claim gives does not hold. What remains is that the href is empty, a placeholder link that leads back to the page itself. Whether such a dead link fails 2.4.4 (its real effect, a reload, is not what text and heading promise) or is a broken link that 2.4.4 does not cover is something competent auditors would split on. They would also split on whether this generic 'no context' claim, made without Rampa reading the destination, names that defect. So I do not confirm it and label it uncertain.

ref: #busca > div > a
subject: iG Mail
message: The text "iG Mail" has at most 3.59:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #f54c31…#f44931), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The "iG Mail" link in the orange header bar. The live CSS sets #busca .ig-email a to color #fff and font-size 13px (regular weight), and the bar's background behind it in the screenshot samples at #f54932 to #f54c30, which gives 3.52:1 to 3.57:1 against white (computed with the WCAG luminance formula). 13px regular text needs 4.5:1 under 1.4.3, so the text fails, as the claim states. The live page has the same markup and style, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The "iG Mail" link in the channel header: white text, 13px, weight 400 (noticias.min.css: #busca .ig-email a{color:#fff;font-size:13px}). The page's inline style gives the header a linear-gradient(90deg,#FF9800,#F44336) background. At the link's position near the right end, that gradient works out to about #F54932, and the screenshot pixels behind the text (245,72-76,48-51) give 3.54-3.59:1, so Rampa's 3.52-3.59:1 is right and below the 4.5:1 that normal-size text needs. I checked the reasons it could pass: it is not large text, and it is not a logotype (it is a plain link label in the site's font, not part of a logo), so the brand-name exception does not apply. The full-page screenshot draws the fixed header near the footer, a stitching artefact, but the colours there match the live CSS, so the capture does not differ in a way that matters.

message: The link text "e-mail" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The "e-mail" item of the site's top navigation bar (visible in the screenshot after "ig mais"), a link to https://minhaconta.ig.com.br/ with title "E-mail". Its list item, which is its programmatically determined context, holds its submenu "Minha conta", "Criar nova conta", "Suporte e-mail". The destination is "iG Minha Conta", a login form for the iG e-mail account (its script validates an e-mail and password). In iG's product menu, the text "E-mail" with that list item tells users the link opens iG's e-mail service, which is where it goes, so the claim that neither the text nor anything around it tells where it goes is not true. The live page has the same link and submenu. The element meets 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The "E-mail" item (CSS shows it as lowercase "e-mail"; title "E-mail") in the iG top navigation bar, next to iG products and channels (último segundo, economia, ..., ig play, ig mais, e-mail, parceiros), as the screenshot shows. It goes to https://minhaconta.ig.com.br/, live titled "iG Minha Conta": the account portal for iG e-mail, which is also what its hover submenu (Minha conta, Criar nova conta, Suporte e-mail, hidden until opened) offers. In this bar the text names iG's e-mail service, which is where the link leads, so its purpose can be determined from the link text alone and it meets 2.4.4; the claim that the text does not tell where it goes is false. The live header has the same item, so the capture does not differ.

ref: #desktop > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > h3
message: The heading "ÚLTIMO SEGUNDO" names a different topic than the content under it.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: An h3 in the site's orange header bar holding a link "Último Segundo" (shown uppercase by CSS) to the channel's home, next to the iG logo, the iG Mail link and search. It names the iG news channel the page belongs to; the content after it (the header tools, then the news article whose h1 follows) is that channel's content, so it does not name a different topic. A site or channel name used as a heading in the banner describes the section it heads; at most the heading level is a structure point, not a 2.4.6 failure. The live HTML has the same h3 and the screenshot shows the bar (drawn lower because it is fixed). The element meets 2.4.6.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The h3 "Último Segundo" (CSS uppercase), a link to https://ultimosegundo.ig.com.br in the channel's orange header bar. Último Segundo is the name of iG's news channel, which publishes this article (the page's domain). The heading identifies that channel, and its section in the snapshot holds the channel bar's tools (iG Mail, the search box) before the article's h1. A channel name is an accurate cue for that section, so it does not name a different topic and the heading meets 2.4.6. The model seems to have read the channel name literally ("last second"). Calling a branding element a heading and its h3 level are questions for 1.3.1, not 2.4.6. The live page has the same heading and header, so the capture does not differ.

ref: #noticia > p:nth-of-type(7) > a
message: The link text "Meta" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: An inline link on the word "Meta" in the article body. Its sentence, which is programmatically determined context, reads (snapshot readingText and live HTML) "O TSE cobrou da Meta tratamento isonômico para os conteúdos políticos das duas campanhas." The link leads to an iG story, "Comitê da Meta vê 'falhas recorrentes' na moderação eleitoral", about Meta's handling of electoral political content (the treatment of Lula's ad accounts), which is what the sentence is about, so the link text with its sentence tells users the link gives more on Meta's treatment of campaign content. The claim that nothing around it tells where it goes is not true of the capture: the sentence does. The paragraph's text field in the snapshot moves the link text to the end ("cobrou da tratamento ... Meta"), but the sentence context was still there. The live page has the same sentence and link (only rel changed from sponsored to nofollow) and the screenshot shows it inline, so the capture does not differ in a way that matters. The element meets 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: An inline link on the word "Meta" in the article body. The paragraph's readingText in the snapshot (and the live HTML) puts it inside the sentence "O TSE cobrou da Meta tratamento isonômico para os conteúdos políticos das duas campanhas", which is the link's programmatically determined context; the packet's ancestor text moves the link word to the end of the paragraph, a quirk of how the text is joined, not of the page. The link goes to the site's own story "Comitê da Meta vê 'falhas recorrentes' na moderação eleitoral", about how Meta moderated election content. The link text plus its sentence point to Meta's handling of the campaigns' political content, which is what the destination covers, so the claim that nothing around it tells where it goes is false and the link meets 2.4.4. The live page has the same sentence and link (only rel changed from sponsored to nofollow), so the capture does not differ in any way that matters. Rampa had both the sentence and the destination title and still judged it wrongly.

ref: #tags > span > a:nth-of-type(2)
message: The link text "LULA" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Último Segundo - Últimas notícias".

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: A tag link "lula" (uppercase by CSS) in the article's "Tags:" row (eleições 2026, lula, presidente...), leading to https://ultimosegundo.ig.com.br/noticias/lula. The destination's static title and heading are the generic "Último Segundo - Últimas notícias", which the capture records truly, but the capture does not show the page's content, so whether it fails to match cannot be told from it. On the live site the page's list is filled by its script, which takes the last segment of the address as the search term (canais.min.js sets options.termos from the /noticias/ path), and iG's content API queried with that term returns Lula news. So the link opens the list of news about Lula, as its text and its tag row say. The generic title is a template title and is what users get too; the tag link is the same live. The element meets 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: A tag link "lula" (CSS uppercase) in the article's "Tags:" row, to https://ultimosegundo.ig.com.br/noticias/lula. The static HTML of that page has the generic title "Último Segundo - Últimas notícias" that Rampa recorded (any /noticias/<term> URL serves the same HTML). But in a browser its script (canais.min.js) reads the term from the URL, changes the list heading to 'ÚLTIMAS NOTÍCIAS COM "lula"' and loads stories filtered by the term; the site's content service, queried with that term, returns Lula stories. The link text, read with its Tags label and its /noticias/lula address, matches a page listing Lula news, so the claim of a mismatch is false and the link meets 2.4.4. The link and the destination's title are the same live as in Rampa's record, which is incomplete rather than wrong. The model had the Tags context and the URL and read a generic title as a mismatch.

message: The text alternative "Contact Us" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
patch.to: Panoramic view of a coastal town by the sea

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the page's top banner (dun_laoghaire.jpg), a photo of the Dún Laoghaire seafront: rocks, the bay, the town and its church spires. It has no text in it, and its alt is "Contact Us". The crop and the screenshot confirm that the image shows nothing like "Contact Us", so the claim holds. The alt does not match the visible h1, which reads "Do you want to find out what's on or book tickets?". Read as a decorative banner, the image must be ignorable by assistive technology (null alt). Read as informative, its alternative should convey the scene. "Contact Us" does neither, so screen readers announce an image named "Contact Us" that is not an equivalent of the picture, and the image fails 1.1.1. The claim, read in good faith, points at that mismatch. The live HTML has the same img and alt, and the screenshot matches the live layout.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the page's banner photo (dun_laoghaire.jpg) with alt "Contact Us". It is not a link. The crop and screenshot show a panorama of the Dun Laoghaire seafront: rocks, sea, terraces and church spires, with no text at all. The claim, that the alternative describes something the image does not show, is true of the capture. I checked for a reason it could pass. No visible "Contact Us" text is drawn on or beside the image (the h1 is "Do you want to find out what's on or book tickets?"), so the alternative is not reproducing text in the image. If the photo is decorative, 1.1.1 requires it to be ignorable by assistive technology, and a non-null alt fails that (F39's test). If it is informative, "Contact Us" does not convey the scene. Either way, the alternative is not an equivalent and the element fails 1.1.1. The claim, read in good faith, points at that mismatch. captureDiffers is no: the live HTML fetched now has the same img, src and alt.

ref: html > head > meta:nth-of-type(5)
subject: width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0 maximum-scale=1
message: The viewport meta element sets maximum-scale=1: in mobile browsers that honor it, people cannot zoom text to 200%.

patch.ref: html > head > meta:nth-of-type(5)
patch.after: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0 maximum-scale=1">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The page's viewport meta element has content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0 maximum-scale=1". The comma between the last two properties is missing, but Blink and WebKit treat whitespace as a separator in viewport content, so maximum-scale=1 still applies. claimTrue: the captured HTML has maximum-scale=1, and the claim limits itself to mobile browsers that honor it. elementFails: the approved ACT rule b4f0c3 (AG WG, mapped to 1.4.4, 'Any failed outcomes: success criterion is not satisfied') fails any maximum-scale value below 2. None of its assumptions holds here: the page has visible content and no other way to resize text. Mobile browsers that honor the property, such as Chrome on Android unless the user turns on Force enable zoom, block pinch zoom past 100%. The rule's accessibility-support note says desktop browsers and many modern mobile browsers ignore the property. That is a known caveat, but it does not change the rule's mapping, which is the mainstream audit reading (axe also tags meta-viewport as wcag144). captureDiffers: I fetched the live page with a desktop and a mobile user agent on 2026-11-21, and both serve the same meta element. The claim names this failure, so the label is true_positive.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the page's meta viewport, content "width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0 maximum-scale=1". A comma is missing before maximum-scale, but the viewport parsing algorithm and browsers treat whitespace as a separator, so maximum-scale=1 is parsed and the claim (mobile browsers that honor it block pinch zoom to 200%) holds; claimTrue yes. The live page sends the same meta to both a desktop and a mobile user agent, and nothing else in the HTML rewrites it, so captureDiffers no. elementFails yes by the approved ACT rule b4f0c3 (Expectation 2: maximum-scale is not less than 2; any failed outcome means 1.4.4 is not satisfied), and Chrome on Android honors it by default unless the user turns on Force enable zoom. The skeptic's reason does hold up in part, though. The same rule's Accessibility Support section says desktop browsers ignore the element and 'most modern mobile browsers either ignore it by default or have an accessibility option which will allow zooming', that the rule 'is not relevant for desktop browsers, nor for most modern mobile browsers', and its Assumptions allow 1.4.4 to be met when another mechanism resizes the text. iOS Safari ignores maximum-scale, desktop zoom works, and Android Chrome offers text scaling and page zoom settings. WCAG 2.1 has no documented failure for this meta, and G142 accepts zoom in commonly available user agents. Competent auditors split on whether this alone fails 1.4.4 (axe and most audit practices fail it; desktop-scoped methodologies and the rule's own support note do not), so the label is uncertain rather than true_positive.

It is a disabled checkbox with nothing to enter, so the claim's premise does not hold for the captured element. elementFails: 2.4.6 asks only that a label describe the control's topic or purpose. In its labelled group and in the cookie dialog, 'Necessary' clearly names the consent category the toggle stands for (necessary cookies). The screenshot shows the visible label next to the switch, and the details view repeats it as 'Necessary (39)' with a description. So the element meets 2.4.6. captureDiffers: the live page has the dialog's Cookiebot styling and loads it through Google Tag Manager, so first-time visitors get the same banner the screenshot shows. The checker had the group name and the neighbouring categories and still judged wrongly, so the cause is model_error.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the disabled, checked 'Necessary' toggle in the Cookiebot consent banner. Its <label for> reads 'Necessary', and it sits in a group named 'Consent Selection' (a visually hidden legend) under the banner heading 'Responsible use of your data', in a visible row with 'Preferences', 'Statistics' and 'Marketing' toggles and 'Show details' (screenshot crop checked). A checkbox takes no typed input: the label only has to say what the choice is, and in that context 'Necessary' names the cookie category the toggle consents to. The toggle is also disabled and permanently on, so the user enters nothing. claimTrue is no because the claim treats the label as failing to say what the control takes, when in its group it does. Understanding 2.4.6 says labels need not be long, 'a word ... may suffice if it provides an appropriate cue', and 'Necessary' is the standard, understood name for this category, so elementFails is no. The script-injected banner cannot be seen in raw HTML, but its standard category labels do not depend on the capture, so captureDiffers is no. The image is the EU common online-pharmacy logo and contains the text "Click to verify if this website is operating legally". Its alt is "psi compliance logo". That describes the picture as a logo. It does not say the link lets users check the pharmacy on the PSI register, and it leaves out the verification text shown in the image. ref: #narrow-by-list
subject: CATEGORY  | BRAND 
message: None of the 2 tabs in this list is exposed as selected: a screen reader does not say which panel is open. Mark the current tab with aria-selected="true" (and the others with "false").

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The layered-navigation filter (#narrow-by-list) is a Magento accordion initialised with "active": false and "collapsible": true. Its script gives it role=tablist with two role=tab headers, Category and Brand. In the capture both tabs have aria-selected=false and aria-expanded=false, both tabpanels are aria-hidden=true, and the screenshot shows both collapsed (chevrons pointing right). It is true that no tab is exposed as selected. But no panel is open, so there is no open panel left unannounced: each header is exposed as collapsed, which matches what sighted users see. The state is programmatically determinable and correct, so the element meets 4.1.2. The live page initialises the same way. The rule requires one selected tab even when every panel is closed, a pattern convention stricter than 4.1.2.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the layered-navigation filter (#narrow-by-list), an accordion built with Magento's collapsible widget, which gives it role=tablist/tab/tabpanel. Its two headers, Category and Brand, are both collapsed: the data-mage-init config sets "active": false, both panels are hidden (aria-hidden=true), and the screenshot shows both closed. Each tab exposes aria-expanded=false and aria-selected=false. The live collapsible.js sets aria-selected and aria-expanded to "true" when a panel opens and to "false" when it closes. So no panel is open, and "none selected" is the true state, which a screen reader reports as collapsed. The claim's statement that a screen reader does not say which panel is open assumes an open panel that does not exist. Marking one tab aria-selected="true" here would misreport the state. 4.1.2 requires that states be programmatically determinable, and they are. The rule applies the APG tabs convention that one tab is always selected, which is stricter than 4.1.2 and does not fit an accordion. The server HTML and config match the capture.
